tldr: This paper theoretically uncovers why contrastive reinforcement learning (CRL) suffers from overestimation in failure-terminated environments (such as falls or collisions) and proposes Safe-CRL, which achieves safe and sustainable goal-reaching using only a one-bit failure termination signal without any extra safety rewards.
hero_caption: An overview of the future occupancy (survival mass) lost to failure termination and the two corrections introduced by Safe-CRL. On the critic side, trajectory-wise normalization distortion is counteracted using mass-weighted InfoNCE; on the actor side, adding the log-survival-mass score restores correct action evaluation.
overview:
In recent years, contrastive reinforcement learning (CRL) has attracted significant attention as a promising framework for goal-conditioned reinforcement learning, as it effectively leverages large-scale neural networks. However, in environments with failure termination—where an episode terminates immediately upon a robot falling or colliding with an obstacle—a fatal issue emerges.

Conventional CRL takes only the pre-failure future states as positive samples and normalizes them so their probabilities sum to 1 for contrastive learning. This is where the pitfall lies. Short trajectories that crash immediately afterward and long trajectories that survive stably are stretched to the exact same weight of 1. As a result, dangerous near-failure trajectories are disproportionately reinforced as successful examples. This triggers unsustainable goal-reaching behaviours—such as rushing into a goal only to immediately topple or crash—and causes learning failures where the policy cannot escape hazardous regions.

To solve this, the authors define the discounted future occupancy removed by failure as survival mass and introduce two minimal corrections based on mathematical derivations. The resulting method, Safe-CRL, applies a mass-weighted MW-InfoNCE loss to the critic and adds a log-survival-mass score obtained from a lightweight predictor to the actor.

Evaluated across 12 robot navigation and locomotion tasks (Brax/MJX environments), Safe-CRL dramatically improves survival time and goal-reaching performance using only a one-bit signal indicating termination, without any additional safety costs or complex constraint engineering. Furthermore, it fully preserves the scaling properties of deep CRL, where performance scales with network depth.
contributions: Theoretically formulated the systematic overestimation bias and policy learning failure mechanisms caused by conventional future relabelling in contrastive reinforcement learning (CRL) under failure termination.

Proposed Safe-CRL with two lightweight and theoretically principled corrections: MW-InfoNCE to fix critic learning distortions, and the log-survival-mass score to restore survival mass in actor updates.
Established a framework that learns safe control policies using only a one-bit signal indicating episode termination, requiring no additional safety annotations or cost functions.

Demonstrated substantially higher survival time and time at goal over the baseline Scaling-CRL across 12 demanding navigation and locomotion tasks, while verifying performance improvements with network depth (scalability).

sections.heading: Why does conventional contrastive RL self-destruct right after reaching the goal?
sections.summary: While contrastive reinforcement learning (CRL) scales well with deeper models, it suffers from crashes and falls immediately after reaching goals in failure-terminated tasks. This section highlights that normalization ignoring the future occupancy lost to failure (survival mass) is the root cause, and introduces the research question.
sections.details:
Scaling up deep learning models to increase policy expressiveness is rapidly growing in importance across reinforcement learning. In goal-conditioned reinforcement learning (GCRL) in particular, contrastive reinforcement learning (CRL)—which casts sparse goal-reaching rewards into a self-supervised contrastive learning objective—is becoming established as a prominent framework that enables scaling through deeper networks.

However, real-world robotic tasks inevitably involve failure termination. In quadruped or humanoid locomotion, falling ends the episode immediately; in navigation or autonomous driving, colliding with an obstacle halts operation on the spot. In such safety-critical environments, agents must not only reach the goal, but also survive (Arrive and Survive). Moreover, in practice, it is ideal to learn purely from a one-bit failure signal indicating termination, without relying on human tuning of safety penalties or extra cost annotations.

Yet conventional CRL, when future trajectories are cut short by failure, simply collects the remaining short steps and renormalizes them so their total probability sums to 1. In other words, it preserves information about what is reachable, but completely discards information about how much future occupancy remains (the survival mass).

This leads to two severe failures. First, catastrophic failure bootstrapping occurs, where abundant short failed trajectories in the early replay buffer are excessively reinforced as positive samples, trapping the agent in unsafe actions. Second, as shown in Figure F2, the agent exhibits unsustainable goal-reaching behaviours, such as rushing toward the goal at high speed only to smash into a wall or topple over immediately afterward. This paper proposes Safe-CRL, an extension that properly restores survival mass to resolve this issue.

captions.F2: Examples of unsustainable goal-reaching seen in conventional Scaling-CRL. (a) The Point agent collides with a moving obstacle right after reaching the goal, (b) Ant rushes into the goal at high speed and crashes into a wall, and (c, d) legged robots topple over immediately upon goal arrival.

sections.heading: Revealed by theory: the missing survival mass and overestimation bias
sections.summary: The authors prove that in an MDP with failure termination, the true Q-value is equivalent to the failure-aware discounted future occupancy. They mathematically reveal how conventional normalization creates a positive overestimation bias that distorts both the critic and the actor.
sections.details:
Here, the theoretical core of the problem is unveiled. As a premise, in an infinite-horizon MDP, the goal-conditioned action-value function (Q-function) is known to match the discounted future state occupancy exactly. However, in environments with a failure termination time $T_f$, things are different.

The authors prove in Proposition 1 that under failure termination, the goal-reaching Q-function strictly equals the failure-aware future goal occupancy $\mu_f^\pi$. Crucially, this $\mu_f^\pi$ is a sub-probability measure whose total mass is strictly less than 1. The authors name this total mass the survival mass $Z^\pi(x)$. Intuitively, it represents the probability that a future step sampled from a geometric distribution falls before failure occurs.

However, conventional CRL extracts only the valid states within an observed short trajectory and divides by their sum (renormalizing to 1) to create positive samples for contrastive learning. The resulting estimate $\hat{Q}_{\text{CRL},g}^\pi(s,a)$ carries a persistent non-negative overestimation bias relative to the true Q-value (amplified by $1/\hat{Z}_\tau \ge 1$) as shown in Equation 12. The shorter the trajectory survival length $L_\tau$, the higher this amplification spikes.

The harmful effects of this normalization manifest separately in both the critic and the actor (see Figure F3):
- Critic side (trajectory-wise normalization distortion): Because short, dangerous trajectories are treated with the exact same weight of 1 as long, safe trajectories, the conditional goal distribution learned by the critic itself becomes distorted (Equation 13).
- Actor side (missing survival mass): Even if the critic's distribution shape were perfectly corrected, contrastive scores can only represent normalized distributions. Because true value decomposes into normalized distribution $\times$ survival mass $Z^\pi(x)$ (Equation 14), the action-dependent survival mass is entirely missing from the actor's objective.

captions.F3: The missing survival mass under failure termination and Safe-CRL's correction approach. While conventional CRL discards post-failure occupancy and forcibly renormalizes, Safe-CRL corrects trajectory weights on the critic side with MW-InfoNCE and adds a log-survival-mass score on the actor side to restore the original unnormalized occupancy.

sections.heading: Safe-CRL: Restoring safety with two minimal corrections
sections.summary: To address the two identified distortions, Safe-CRL introduces MW-InfoNCE to weight InfoNCE by realized survival mass on the critic side, and adds a predicted log-survival-mass score on the actor side. The only extra cost is adding one lightweight Z-encoder.
sections.details:
Once the theoretical cause is identified, the solution is remarkably simple and elegant. The paper introduces two corrections.

### 3.1 Critic correction: mass-weighted InfoNCE (MW-InfoNCE)
If each trajectory was divided by its realized survival mass $\hat{Z}_i$ during positive sample creation, the idea is to multiply the entire row of the contrastive loss back by that same $\hat{Z}_i$ (Equation 15). As proven in Proposition 2, this weighting neatly cancels out trajectory-wise normalization skew in expectation, allowing the critic to learn a conditional distribution with the exact same shape as the true occupancy.

### 3.2 Actor correction: log-survival-mass correction
Even when the critic captures the correct normalized occupancy $\bar{\mu}_f^\pi$, obtaining the true value requires multiplying by the survival mass $Z^\pi(x)$. In the log-density-ratio domain, this simply corresponds to adding $\log Z^\pi(x)$ (Corollary 1, Equation 18). This aligns the actor's action ranking perfectly with the true failure-aware Q-value.

### 3.3 Implementation and training the Z-encoder
To implement these corrections, the authors introduce a lightweight network, the Z-encoder $Z_\psi(s,a) \in (0, 1)$, which predicts survival mass from state and action. It is trained via Monte Carlo estimation using a binary cross-entropy loss (Equation 19) on a binary label $Y_t$ indicating whether failure occurred before horizon $H_t$ sampled from a geometric distribution. When updating the actor, $\log Z_\psi(s,a)$ is added to the contrastive score, propagating gradients through the Z-encoder back to the action input.

One might wonder: why not just include failure as an absorbing terminal state in the contrastive learning output space? However, because the failure state is shared across all anchors, negative sampling breaks down, and it cannot serve as an actor's target goal anyway. Safe-CRL's design—leaving the goal space clean and externally restoring only survival mass—is exceptionally well-reasoned.

sections.heading: Testing capabilities across 12 demanding robot tasks
sections.summary: Performance is evaluated across 12 Point, Car, Ant, and Humanoid tasks built with Brax/MJX. Challenging conditions prone to falling are created by lowering ground friction and limiting actuator outputs, and Safe-CRL is compared against the Scaling-CRL baseline.
sections.details:
To evaluate the proposed method, 12 navigation and locomotion tasks were set up on the Brax physics simulator with the MJX backend (Figure F4).
- Navigation (Point Goal, Car Goal): Tasks derived from Safety-Gymnasium where entering moving obstacles (gremlins) or hazardous zones (pitfalls) causes immediate failure termination. New goals respawn upon reaching the target.
- Legged locomotion (Ant, Humanoid): Task suites from Scaling-CRL (Goal, Maze, Pitfall) where falling terminates the episode immediately. In pitfall tasks, entering danger zones also causes termination. To make failure even more likely, ground sliding friction was drastically reduced from the standard 1.0 to 0.6, and Humanoid actuator gears were lowered to create slippery, fall-prone dynamics.

The observation space includes 2D LiDAR readings (accounting for occlusions) to detect walls and obstacles. The comparison baseline is Scaling-CRL, a strong contrastive baseline scaled with deeper networks under identical conditions (comparisons with SAC-HER are also included in the appendix). The networks primarily use 64-layer deep ResNet architectures (8 layers for Point/Car), with Safe-CRL adding only a 4-layer Z-encoder.

Three evaluation metrics are used:
1. Time at goal: Number of steps spent remaining inside the goal area. This is the primary metric reflecting both arrival speed and subsequent safety maintenance.
2. Survival time: Number of steps survived until failure termination or the time limit (1000 steps).
3. Goal coverage: Proportion of episodes where the agent reached the goal at least once.

captions.F4: The 12 robot environments used in the experiments. They span diverse failure-terminated tasks, from 2D navigation with Point and Car to advanced locomotion tasks with Ant and Humanoid traversing slippery floors, pitfalls (blue columns), and mazes.

sections.heading: Overwhelming survival capability and emergent advanced avoidance behaviours
sections.summary: Safe-CRL achieved higher time at goal and survival time than the baseline across all 12 tasks. Scalability with deeper networks was maintained, and advanced safe avoidance behaviours such as backward walking, deceleration, and wide detours emerged autonomously.
sections.details:
Benchmark results were striking. Across all 12 evaluated tasks, Safe-CRL achieved higher average time at goal and average survival time than Scaling-CRL.

Improvements were especially prominent in difficult, fall-prone tasks. For instance, in Ant Goal, time at goal jumped more than 2.4-fold from 276.8 steps to 684.0 steps; in Humanoid Goal, it improved from 22.2 to 266.4 steps, and in Humanoid Big Pitfall from 8.2 to 474.1 steps. While Scaling-CRL often had high goal coverage, its survival times were extremely short—falling into unsustainable goal-reaching where agents crash and burn upon arrival. Safe-CRL completely overcomes this weakness.

Furthermore, when testing depth scaling (from depth 4 to 256 layers), Safe-CRL preserved the scalability where time at goal and survival time increase as networks get deeper. Remarkably, an 8-layer Safe-CRL achieved performance competitive with or better than a 64-layer Scaling-CRL, showing exceptional sample efficiency.

Visualizing the learned policy behaviours (Figure F8) revealed surprisingly sophisticated actions despite learning from only a one-bit failure signal:
- The Point robot brakes and executes an S-curve replanning maneuver to weave between moving obstacles.
- The Humanoid walks backward to reach a goal behind it without falling, and recovers balance after oversteering into a goal.
- In Pitfall environments, robots alter their trajectories well in advance to take wide detours around hazards or carefully decelerate when squeezing through narrow gaps.

captions.F8: Execution snapshots of policies learned by Safe-CRL. Sophisticated safe behaviours are visible, including dynamic obstacle avoidance by Point, backward walking and fall recovery by Humanoid, and long-horizon planning taking wide detours around dense pitfalls.

sections.heading: What makes it work? A thorough ablation of components
sections.summary: Ablation experiments reveal that performance gains are primarily driven by the actor-side log-survival-mass correction. Evaluating the weighting coefficient β also confirms that the theoretically derived setting (β=1) functions with balanced performance.
sections.details:
To isolate the roles of Safe-CRL's two corrections (MW-InfoNCE and the log-survival-mass correction), ablation experiments were conducted (Table 1).

The results showed that MW-InfoNCE alone provided only marginal improvements over Scaling-CRL; the bulk of the performance gain stemmed from the actor's log-survival-mass correction ($\log Z$ correction). For example, in Humanoid Goal, MW-InfoNCE alone reached a time at goal of only 28.3 steps, whereas applying the $\log Z$ correction alone increased it substantially to 288.7 steps. Consistent with the theory in Section 2, this confirms that fixing the critic's normalization distortion alone is insufficient—directly reflecting survival mass in the actor's policy update is critically important.

Experiments also varied the weight coefficient $\beta$ for log-survival mass in the actor objective (theoretically $\beta=1.0$) across 0.2, 1.0, and 5.0. While larger $\beta$ values tended to increase survival time, the trade-off with goal-reaching performance depended on the environment. In Safe-CRL, fixing $\beta=1$ as directly derived from theory yields robust results without ad-hoc hyperparameter tuning, which is a major practical benefit.

sections.heading: Conclusion: A new standard for safety in self-supervised RL
sections.summary: In contrastive reinforcement learning with failure termination, preserving total occupancy lost to termination is just as crucial as capturing relative relationships among observed futures. Safe-CRL achieves this at minimal extra cost, setting a new benchmark for scalable safe RL.
sections.details:
This paper mathematically identified that normalization ignoring lost survival mass in contrastive reinforcement learning under failure termination leads to a systematic overestimation bias. It then introduced Safe-CRL, combining two simple corrections: mass-weighted InfoNCE for the critic and a log-survival-mass score for the actor.

Without requiring complex Constrained MDP (CMDP) formulations or reward-engineered safety costs, Safe-CRL dramatically improved survival time and goal-reaching performance relying solely on a one-bit signal indicating episode termination. It provides an essential insight to the community for self-supervised RL in the large-model era: one must restore not only the distribution of observed future states, but also the absolute magnitude of lost occupancy.

sections.heading: Distinction from related work: positioning relative to constrained RL and survival models
sections.summary: Building on HER, C-learning, and Scaling-CRL, this section clarifies critical differences from Constrained MDPs (CMDPs) and survival analysis approaches. Safe-CRL's novelty lies in correcting distortions while fully preserving the CRL representation framework.
sections.details:
Related work surrounding this paper broadly falls into three lines:

1. Goal-conditioned RL and contrastive RL (GCRL / CRL):
Foundational future relabelling techniques like HER, CRL formulating this as density ratio estimation, and Scaling-CRL enabling deeper architectures. Other works like USHER correct selection bias from stochastic dynamics, but no prior work addressed the fundamental challenge of missing survival mass under failure termination.

2. Survival analysis-based RL (SVL / SRL):
Approaches like SVL modeling time-to-termination and SRL modeling goal dwell-time have been proposed recently. These represent different approaches that directly model time-to-event distributions. In contrast, Safe-CRL removes overestimation while preserving CRL's powerful framework of occupancy and density ratio estimation.

3. Constrained Markov Decision Processes (CMDP):
The standard paradigm in safe RL, including CPO and Lagrangian multiplier methods, which treats safety as cumulative cost constraints. However, these do not assume that hazardous events immediately end the episode, and they require explicit cost function design. Safe-CRL operates purely on a one-bit termination signal, making it far easier to deploy in practice.

sections.heading: Appendix: Computational cost, comparisons with TD learning, and remaining challenges
sections.summary: The appendix details that the added Z-encoder adds only a 2.8% computational overhead, shows that Monte Carlo estimation is more stable than TD learning, and discusses remaining limitations regarding spatial exploration bias.
sections.details:
The appendix reports important supplementary experimental data concerning implementation and practical utility:

- Low computational overhead:
Compared to the 64-layer deep actor and critic, the added Z-encoder has only 4 layers. Parameter count increases by only about 4.2%, and wall-clock training time increases by just 2.8% per 100M environment steps (from 9.07 to 9.32 hours), making it exceptionally cheap to adopt (Table D.2).

- Why Monte Carlo estimation over TD learning:
An alternative using TD learning (Clipped Double-Q) to estimate survival mass $Z(s,a)$ was evaluated (Figure D.3), but caused significant performance drops in Car Goal and Humanoid Goal. Binary classification (Monte Carlo estimation) based on failure truncation before a geometrically sampled step proved substantially more stable for learning.

- Exploration limitations (Figure F9):
While Safe-CRL cleanly fixes value evaluation distortions, it does not resolve the spatial exploration bias inherent to CRL. As shown in Figure F9, spatial asymmetries in goal-reaching success rates remain for goals located far from the initial position or in blind spots. Integrating with more efficient exploration methods based on safe state representations remains an important direction for future work.

captions.F9: Heatmap of success rates across different goal locations in the playground (darker colors indicate lower success rates). Variations in learning progress depend on distance from the initial position (diamond marker) and geometric layouts, illustrating that restoring survival mass alone cannot fully eliminate uneven exploration.

takeaways: Applying conventional contrastive RL (CRL) in failure-terminated environments causes short failed trajectories to be overestimated, reinforcing behaviours that crash or fall immediately after reaching the goal.

Because the true value function decomposes into the product of normalized occupancy and survival mass, mathematically exact corrections require only two adjustments: InfoNCE row-weighting for the critic and log-survival-mass addition for the actor.
Safe behaviours can be acquired using only a one-bit signal indicating failure termination, without complex safety cost functions or hyperparameter tuning.
Computational overhead is only about 2.8% in training time, and CRL's key advantage of performance scaling with deeper networks is fully maintained.
limitations: Does not directly address safety costs that do not terminate the episode (such as continuous minor penalties or CMDP-style constraints).
Right-censoring caused by episode time limits is not handled perfectly; all samples surviving up to the time limit are treated as surviving.
Does not resolve the intrinsic exploration bias of CRL (uneven reachability for distant or obstructed goals), leaving combination with advanced exploration mechanisms as future work.
